inline.s: They too hang up the sign of believing in the Buddha, but they are wholly unaware that the Medicine Buddha Sutra, in its very opening, has explained in detail the sin of miserliness and the refusal to part with anything. The sutra says: “There are sentient beings who do not recognize good and evil, who harbour only greed and stinginess, who know not how to give, nor the retribution of giving; foolish and without wisdom, deficient in the root of faith, they amass much wealth and treasure, diligently guarding it. When a beggar comes, their heart is displeased; and if they must give, it is like cutting the flesh of their own body, and the heart engenders painful regret. Such people, at the end of life, are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, or in the animal realm.” Because the very wealthy have more wealth than they need and no use for keeping it themselves, and though they know clearly that many people will starve to death, they still refuse to give their wealth to relieve them. If one reproaches them from the standpoint of morality, this is simply indirect murder. The one who has accumulated the most money and wields the greatest power, and yet refuses to give — the crime of murder he bears is the heavier for it. For example, seeing a child standing at the edge of a well, about to fall in; a person stands beside it, says not a word, does not pull the child back, and lets it fall into the well and die. We would surely say that the child has been killed by him. And the rich man's seeing a calamity and not rescuing is just the same. How much more so when, being so wealthy, he will not part even with a small portion of the interest — then the thousands upon thousands of starving people who die on the roads, must they not be counted as killed by him? How can the crime of killing thousands and tens of thousands be done away with by a mind of arrogance, using belief in the Buddha as a front, grudgingly spending a little of the money he cannot use up, and doing a few good deeds done only for show, and thinking that he has thereby already performed merit and may escape all his sins? I think I fear that heaven and earth, ghosts and gods, would never so vaguely forgive him. So I say this passage of fact is precisely to hope that everyone can tell the true from the false, break open the miserliness within the heart, and in no case repeat the mistake of amassing wealth without giving!

The great Russian writer Tolstoy once said: “People in present-day society, when a million enters by the left hand and they give away one or two yuan by the right, call themselves great philanthropists.” From this one can see that such conduct is a common disease of the world. But for the ordinary run of people it is excusable; for those who believe in the Buddha, it should be earnestly corrected. Everyone must arouse a true heart of compassion and relieve all the suffering of our fellow beings; take the recitation of the Buddha's name and the cultivation of wisdom as the principal practice, and the vigorous performance of all kinds of good deeds — saving people and building merit — as the assisting practice; so that, in accord with Buddhist Dharma, one cultivates both blessedness and wisdom, with the principal and the assisting clearly distinguished. Let me now briefly conclude the above and set it out in items:
1. The wealthy I have seen over the past several decades — their descendants have all declined;
2. Over the past sixty years (this article was written in
), the great families of civil and military officials have all declined, and their descendants no longer flourish;
3. Only the few great officials who refused to amass wealth — their descendants can still pursue their studies and make progress;

4. Those whose offices were highest, whose opportunities for wealth were the greatest, and who yet refused to become wealthy and had their thoughts always on relieving the multitude — their descendants flourished most prosperously and most enduringly; every one of these is attested by historical fact;

5. Of the several instances cited above — the families with thirty million, forty million, and several hundred million — all of a sudden, in a single day, everything was emptied; these were all families that refused to do deeds of relief and goodness;

6. The very wealthy, caring only for their own lavish enjoyment, amassing money to leave to their descendants, and when famine comes refusing to give out a great sum to relieve the calamity, are no different from committing the crime of murder, and are subject to moral condemnation and the sway of karmic retribution;

7. The heavenly principle of Buddhism lies in everyone's heart. Whom everyone thanks, heaven delights in; what everyone resents and is angry at, heaven is angry at. The ancients said: “Pointed at by a thousand men, one dies without illness”; the Book of History says: “Heaven's seeing comes from the seeing of the people; heaven's hearing comes from the hearing of the people.” (Heaven's seeing and hearing come from the seeing and hearing of the people.) The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “If one causes sentient beings to rejoice, then one causes all the Tathagatas to rejoice.” Therefore, to seek blessing, one must create blessing for others; otherwise, neither the Buddha nor heaven can do anything;

8. If the wealthy, in praying to the gods and worshipping the Buddha, burning incense and reciting sutras, do not arouse a great heart of compassion and give wealth to relieve the multitude, they still will not be in accord with Buddhist Dharma.

In sum, the method of preserving wealth must employ a wise perception, that is, a far-seeing vision and a vast capacity of mind. The several figures mentioned above, such as Lord Fan Wenzheng, belong to this class. As for the rest, who are not adept at preserving wealth — the world is full of them, vast as a flood! They cannot keep their descendants rich and prosperous long, only because their own wisdom is insufficient: they can see one point yet miss ten thousand aspects; they see only the surface and not the inner content. To put it simply, when they look at an almanac they see only the first day and do not know that tomorrow is the second, and far less know that at the year's end there is a last night. But though such foolish people are many, there are also not a few persons of karmic roots in society; once a point is made to them, they can at once awaken, and the perception of wisdom will suddenly open bright.

As for what the wise course of action is, please savor the two sayings in Laozi's Daodejing: “When one works for others, the more he possesses; when one gives to others, the more he has.” The several examples of Lord Fan Wenzheng and the others related in this piece are the annotations to these two sayings. Know that Laozi is one of the world's most supreme philosophers. His political, economic, and military learning are all exceedingly exalted, and his philosophy of life cannot be shaken by any age. Among the essential meanings of Laozi's doctrine there is the saying: “The reverse is the movement of the Way.” The gist is that one should turn back — this is the motive for a sudden awakening; most of his whole book is devoted to explaining this principle. Let me cite two more lines: “Know the male, but keep to the female, and be the ravine of the world; know the white, but keep to the black, and be the model of the world.” The male is, for instance, being rich and powerful, and able to be proud — what everyone covets; only the wise person, in reverse, seeks to avoid such dazzling blaze, and exerts himself toward the plain and lowly, to escape others' jealousy. The phrase “be the ravine of the world” means that the multitude will, on the contrary, submit to him. The word “white” means, for instance, holding high office, enjoying a great name, dignity and glory, which others envy — this too is what everyone seeks without obtaining. But the wise person, in reverse, seeks to avoid dignity and glory, exerting himself to hide his brightness, to nurture obscurity, to yield and to be humble. The Doctrine of the Mean says: “One wears brocade but still puts on an overgarment, disliking that its pattern be too conspicuous.” For example, wearing a garment of fine brocade, one still puts an outer garment over it, unwilling to let the brocade show to the outside. This shows that the gentleman genuinely practices goodness and righteousness, and does not pursue empty reputation, in order to avoid producing a negative influence; such a person is the more esteemed by society. These views are all contrary to this worldly opinion. In other words, going against emotional desire in order to accord with reason — such words most people will not take in, or they think it is talking about astronomy and cannot understand it. Yet there are many people in society with wise eyes, and they will surely approve.

blocks.text: The Method of Preserving Wealth, the Middle Part

inline.s: What is the Way of heaven? The Book of Changes says: “One yin and one yang is what is called the Way.” This yin and yang is not empty and shadowy; every one of them can be supported by fact. For instance, where there is day there must be night; where there is cold there must be heat; where there is spring and summer there is autumn and winter; where there is tide rising there is tide falling. Observed from these phenomena of nature, each is one fullness and one emptiness, one waning and one waxing. Extending this principle to human affairs, it is likewise. For example, the one prosperity and one decline of human affairs, one suffering and one joy, one sorrow and one gladness, one order and one disorder. But the yin and yang of the seasons has a fixed standard, unchanging through ten thousand ages; whereas the prosperity and decline of human affairs, following the movements of the human heart, changes without regularity. This changeless change is nevertheless drawn along by the fixed standard of the Way of heaven's one yin and one yang.

Let me try to put it thus: if a person loves pride and arrogance, there will surely come a time when he suddenly collapses; if a person loves idleness and ease, there will surely come days of extreme hardship; if a person loves miserliness and greed for money, there will surely be descendants who squander in debauchery and gambling to ruin him; if a person loves cunning and scheming, there will surely be dull and foolish descendants to be cheated by others. These changing human affairs — a wise person will naturally notice and see them, and know that the principle is the same as the rising and setting of the sun and moon, and the coming and going of cold and heat. The Way of heaven is a diagram of the Great Ultimate: half is black, half is white, and in the middle there is a boundary; once one crosses this boundary the yin and yang lose their balance, and change begins. This is called: when yang reaches its extreme, yin is born; when yin reaches its extreme, yang is born. In other words, what reaches the height of prosperity must decline, and what reaches the depth of adversity must grow.

The great sages from ancient times down to the present have all been able to see into and understand this principle, so they teach people always to place themselves in the position of suffering loss, that is, to be humble and yielding, to give away wealth without greediness, to restrain oneself and benefit others. Among the common run, people without learning are certainly unwilling to do such loss-suffering matters. From the standpoint of the new-style scholars, they would even mock this and call it a negative morality. Know that all great and positive undertakings are brought forth by these persons of negative morality: for only by negatively restraining oneself can one positively benefit others; only by giving away wealth without greediness can one further public benefit; only by being humble and yielding can one be the more esteemed and admired by others, and one's undertakings the more smooth and easy to succeed. In the beginning it seems to be suffering loss, but in the end one still gains great advantage.

People of shallow views and ignorance can only see the surface of all things, and cannot see the opposite side of things. For example, as in chess, they see only one move and not the second or third. They do not know that the affairs of the world are all a game of chess: if I move one move, the opponent must answer me with a move, and immediately a second and a third follow. Buddhism clearly explains the principle of one cause and one fruit, and of response — truly the world's highest science and philosophy. I use chess as a metaphor: when we say a word or do a thing, we are making a move against other people; when we speak and act, the resolve we hold in our hearts is a move against Heaven; all people and all things are our chess opponents.

If we show kindness to a dog, the dog will wag its tail at us to show affection; if we speak harshly to it, it will droop its tail and walk away. As for people, that goes without saying! If I treat others with humility and generosity, they will be grateful; if I treat others with pride and harshness, they will bear resentment in their hearts — and this is still a small opponent. If we bully those who are without ability, or harbour the intent to harm people, or use clever means to take advantage of others so that they suffer loss without realizing it; or, relying on a privileged position, such as being an official or the manager of a company, secretly seek private profit; or, being wealthy, refuse to relieve calamity while comfortably lying at home in luxury — these matters, the multitude can indeed do nothing about, and the law cannot reach him; he has won the game, and his opponents on the other side have all lost. But the Way of heaven does not permit him to win, and will act as the great opponent on behalf of the multitude; Heaven needs only to make a slight move and his whole board of pieces seems to have turned to stone, and in the end he is utterly defeated. This is called: “A man has a thousand reckonings, Heaven has but one.” We are every day playing chess against people, but in reality we are playing chess against Heaven; if we win the greater against people, we lose the more severely against Heaven. Conversely, if we are willing to concede a little to people, and everywhere help others out a move, so as to keep them from losing, then my own game will not be greatly lost either, and on the contrary I shall win a very great game against Heaven!

The Lord Fan Wenzheng spoken of above is the clearest example: he was originally very poor, and served as minister and general for several decades, and yet when he died he still had no private fields, gardens, or estates. Viewed through the eyes of worldly people, he may be said to have toiled in vain his whole life. Yet he won a great game against Heaven, and his children and grandchildren were for the most part noble, flourishing, and talented! The others, such as Lord Yelü Wenzheng, Lord Lin Wenzhong, and Lord Zeng Wenzheng, were all willing to lose the game, and in the end all won a great game of chess against Heaven. And those many persons who were skilled at winning the game, who made hundreds of thousands, millions, tens of millions, and hundreds of millions, were in the end moved against by a single move of Heaven and lost it all. The ancients said: “Man can conquer Heaven, and Heaven's decree can likewise conquer man.” Heaven's decree is a fixed principle of heaven. The law of yin and yang demands balance; when people do things to excess, they have lost the balance. Because our hearts first violate the middle harmony of the law of yin and yang, a reaction arises, and we are disciplined by the law of yin and yang, and made to return to the state of balance. When Heaven plays chess, it moves neither heart nor hand, and yet people naturally lose. For example, throw a ball against a wall and the ball naturally rebounds; the harder it is thrown, the harder it rebounds, and the wall itself has not moved nor exerted any effort nor lost the least bit. So the Book of History says: “The calamity Heaven makes, one may still avoid; the calamity one makes oneself, one cannot survive.” Mencius says: “What you send out to others returns to you.” The meaning is: one creates one's own karma and receives one's own retribution; this is the same principle as the Buddhist scriptures' “one makes one's own causes, one reaps one's own fruits.”

And what is called man conquering Heaven is not truly conquering Heaven; it means that when a person, following Heaven's fixed principle, holds his heart in doing things, in the end he will obtain the later victory. One originally poor afterward becomes prosperous; one originally burdened with anxiety afterward attains peace and joy. Such a victory is the victory of heavenly principle. Although I say that the virtuous man wins a game against Heaven, in reality it is Heaven that wins; know that the Way of heaven can never lose. The balance of the Way of heaven's one yin and one yang is the Middle Way, also called the middle harmony; the Doctrine of the Mean says: “When the middle harmony is achieved, heaven and earth are in their places, and all things are nourished.” If the human affairs of the world lose their peace and harmony, they stir up changes in the Way of heaven: just as the great calamities of war and famine are caused by the injustice of human affairs and the disharmony of the human heart. Strife between man and man, between nation and nation, between party and party — whatever the temporary victory or defeat, the outcome is still mutual ruin; even the temporarily victorious will in the end be defeated. Look through the histories of the nations of the world and you will know that those who won the game were, after all, also losers; and from this one knows that heavenly principle is ultimately just. The inequity and disharmony of the human heart will in the end be judged and corrected by heavenly principle.

Among the humans of the world, the numbers of men and women are forever balanced. There is a family surnamed Zhang whose mother bore ten sons, and a family surnamed Li whose mother bore ten daughters, so that summing the whole world's count, the numbers of men and women will not differ greatly. This proves the justice of the Way of heaven and the middle harmony of yin and yang, with a power of inconceivable, natural adjustment. If we wish to rely on our abilities to violate the balancing power of heavenly principle, in the end we shall surely suffer the consequences ourselves. If heavenly principle and yin and yang had no force of judgment and adjustment, then the numbers of men and women would never remain forever balanced, and everything in the world would forever lose its justice: the strong and the clever would be forever rich and noble, and the good would never again lift up their heads. The world would fall into great disorder, and calamity would descend.

Europeans and Americans observe heavenly principle with short-sighted eyes, thinking that in the world only the strong and the clever will be victorious, and that the peaceable and cowardly should be subdued by others, so they call it “the survival of the fittest.” This incomplete doctrine has led people of the world into pride and evil-doing: pride means having support and so being without fear — I have power and am not afraid of you, and so I put on airs and display my might; fullness means having to use up one's power, and having to exhaust one's happiness, caring only for one's own private profit and not planning for others, caring only for present pleasure and not providing for future concerns. The ambitious aggressions of Germany, Japan, and other countries were led astray by just such doctrines!

The Way of heaven is a very simple matter: that which is excessive is disciplined; that which suffers loss is made up. The teachings of the sages of China — the Confucian, Buddhist, and Laozi-Zhuangzi schools — all repeatedly enjoin and make clear this principle. The Book of Changes says: “The Way of heaven diminishes the full and benefits the humble; the Way of earth transforms the full and flows onward to the humble; ghosts and gods bring calamity to the full and bless the humble; the Way of man hates the full and loves the humble.” The Book of History says: “Fullness brings loss, humility gains, this is the Way of heaven.” It also says: “Only Heaven blesses the good and sends calamity upon the licentious.” The opposite of the word “licentious” is “good.” The meaning of the word “good” is exceedingly broad; if one wishes to define it precisely, all the virtues contain the meaning of the humble virtue, and all take the humble virtue as their basis. The Book of Changes is the book that explains the Way of heaven; the two hexagrams Heaven and Earth are a general account of the purport of the Way of heaven. The hexagram Heaven says: “Able to benefit the world without speaking of what it benefits” — this is the meaning of the humble virtue. The hexagram Earth says: “Though the Earth has its beauty, it conceals it and follows in the service of the king, not daring to take credit.” The way of this line is: to not reveal one's talent, not lay claim to merit and fame, that is, not to pursue reputation and not to boast of achievement — this too is the meaning of the humble virtue. The Diamond Sutra says: having saved all beings, one feels that one has not yet saved them. It also says: giving to relieve the multitude, one is not conscious of having given. This is the world's highest morality, and it contains the humble virtue within it.

Furthermore, filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame — these are all weighted toward a sense of duty and light toward a sense of right. And the sense of duty is to feel that one still has an obligation to fulfill toward others; this is humility. The evil-doers of the world are simply those whose sense of right is heavy and who lack the sense of duty. As the old saying puts it, to value profit and make light of righteousness is exactly the opposite of the humble virtue. Therefore all morality lies within the humble virtue: setting out from humility, toward parents and brothers it is filial piety and brotherly respect; toward society and the multitude it is loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame. All people are respectful and glad toward the humble virtue and good deeds, and resentful, angry, and secretly hateful toward pride, fullness, and evil deeds. As for Heaven's sending down blessing and calamity, it is called the Way of heaven, yet in reality it is human feeling; it is called Heaven's sending down, yet in reality it is brought about by oneself! It was said above that the Way of heaven is the expression of human affairs; the Book of History says: “Heaven's seeing comes from the seeing of the people; heaven's hearing comes from the hearing of the people.” The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “If one causes sentient beings to rejoice, then one causes all the Tathagatas to rejoice.” Therefore, when we do good and add blessing to others, we of ourselves receive that blessing; when we do evil and add harm to others, we of ourselves receive that calamity. From this one knows that all the people and all the things facing us are Heaven; everywhere there is heavenly principle within them. Apart from this, there is no other place for heavenly principle to be expressed.

Then, when we act, speak, arise in thought, and show our countenance toward them, we must be especially careful and cautious. Though they may be foolish, or timid, or aged and weak, orphans and widows without anyone to help them; if we bully them, then in the not-distant future I myself or my descendants will likewise be foolish, timid, solitary, and widowed, and be bullied by others. Conversely, if toward these powerless and pitiable people we harbour compassion and moreover devise ways to help them, afterwards I too shall receive others' help, and my descendants will never be foolish, timid, solitary, and widowed, nor bullied by others. This karmic retribution of the cycle of heavenly principle — a person of wise perception can naturally observe it family by family in society, and can even more prove it in the outcomes of every good and evil man in history. This is also one of the most important things in social science!
Written by Yuntai while ill, June 1942

blocks.text: The Method of Preserving Wealth, the Lower Part

inline.s: Last spring (1942) I wrote the two articles, the upper and middle parts, of The Method of Preserving Wealth, and sent them to the monthly Luohan Cai for publication; afterwards, because I fell ill and took to my bed, I could not continue to write the lower part. This spring, through the efforts of Messrs. Rong Baiyun and Huang Jingwan, the article was again sent for publication in the Shen Bao, and was quite appreciated by the readers, and many people contributed money to print it in a single volume; but because they had not seen the lower part, they felt it a pity.

My original plan in writing the lower part was to gather examples of the ancients doing good and accumulating virtue, by which they enabled their descendants to be rich, noble, and illustrious, as corroboration. Lately, in compiling the Memorial Volume for My Late Mother, the Honourable Lady Chongde, I respectfully recounted the excellent words and noble deeds of several generations of ancestors, and in particular wrote the article “The Karmic Retribution of the Meritorious Deeds of the Seventh-generation Ancestor Leshan Gong in Practicing Medicine to Benefit the World.” The seventh-generation ancestor Leshan Gong gave up himself to benefit others, and for two hundred years many generations of my family's descendants have received the shelter of his blessedness and virtue, so it can serve as a most fitting corroborating material for this article. Though this is after all a private family matter, the meritorious deeds of Leshan Gong were once published in the book of the Prefecture and County Gazetteer, and they were moreover honoured and valued by the worthy and learned of the society of that time; the good deeds of several generations of ancestors also have historical material by which they may be verified, and can be said to be enough to win the confidence of the public; they are exactly the evidence for The Method of Preserving Wealth, so to take them as the lower part should, I think, gain the readers' acceptance.

I often examine myself: the time at which I heard the principles of the sages was already late, and the time at which I knew my own faults was already too late. Recalling what I have done in my life, the sins and faults I have committed are too numerous to list — truly I am ashamed before my ancestors, my parents, heaven and earth, ghosts and gods! And now I am already old and declining, and illness clings to me, and I feel even more that I lack the courage and strength to make amends; I fear deeply that the virtue and grace of my ancestors will fall from me, and be lost in obscurity forever; therefore I respectfully record the virtues of my ancestors in order to tell later generations, so that everyone may obtain some warning, enlightenment, and encouragement, to make up a little for my faults.

At first I did not dare to publish this article to the world; it was wholly because friends urged and required me, again and again, to be sure to complete the full text of The Method of Preserving Wealth, that I at last dared to bring it out for publication, and I hope to have something to answer for toward the readers.
Written by Nie Yuntai while ill, April 1943

blocks.text: Appendix 1: The Karmic Retribution of the Meritorious Deeds of the Seventh-generation Ancestor Leshan Gong, Who Practiced Medicine to Benefit the World
(1) The Good Deeds of Leshan Gong

inline.s: My family's ancestral home was in Jiangxi, and it was only from the ninth-generation ancestor Qilong Gong that we moved to Hengshan in Hunan. The seventh-generation ancestor Leshan Gong was born in the eleventh year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, that is, in the year 1672. His accumulation of learning was profound and his essays were very good, yet he did not sit the examinations; instead he followed his grandfather in studying medicine, and opened a small medicine shop. Because his medical skill was excellent and moreover he loved to do good and give, his name as a physician became great. Later, because the shop was robbed, he closed it, and even mortgaged the house he lived in to repay a debt, temporarily moving to the countryside. The local officials and gentry, because Leshan Gong, in practicing medicine to save people, met with this misfortune, then pooled money to help him redeem his original house, and helped him rent a room to open a medicine shop.

In the forty-second year of the Kangxi reign, that is, the year 1703, a great plague broke out in Hengshan, and those who sought treatment came day and night without cease, and thus very many were saved. And Leshan Gong relieved the poor and the prisoners especially abundantly. The then county magistrate, a man named Ge, on account of Leshan Gong's abundant virtue and wide learning, specially invited him to serve as his aide in the yamen, and said to Leshan Gong: “You hold the intention of saving people, and I have no way to repay you; let me have your son study and become famous, as a return for your benefiting the world and saving people.” Leshan Gong accepted Magistrate Ge's suggestion and sent his son Xiantao into the Wenfeng and Jixian academies to study. Before long, Xiantao passed the provincial examination as a juren, and subsequently passed the metropolitan examination as a jinshi.

Leshan Gong was then sixty-seven years old, and escorted his son to the capital to sit the metropolitan examination. Passing a place called Shekou, he happened upon a plague breaking out in the depth of winter, and those patients treated by Leshan Gong all recovered immediately. When Leshan Gong was seventy-four, he again led his son to the capital, waiting for an appointment. Traveling north by the Grand Canal, many of the grain-boat workers had caught an infectious disease, and those treated by Leshan Gong all recovered at once. This spread among all the grain boats, and many sick people on the boats called out at the side of his vessel, and used ropes to tie up the boat Leshan Gong travelled in, so that the boat could not move on. Leshan Gong could not bear to watch people die without saving them, so he instructed his son Xiantao to change to land travel, hire a mule-litter and hurry to the capital, while he himself stayed to continue treating and saving people. After several months, when the epidemic had ceased, he then reached the capital.

At this time, Xiantao had just been appointed magistrate of Zhen'an County in Shaanxi Province, and so Leshan Gong accompanied his son to his post. After arriving in Zhen'an County, he instructed the mountain-dwelling people to gather herbs on the spot to increase their income. The next year, after he returned to his home in Hengshan, Hunan, he sent a letter to his son, teaching him the methods and principles of loving the people and administering the region. The words of the letter were earnest and sincere, and when it was seen by his son's superior, the Shaanxi Governor Chen Wengong, it was greatly praised. He had this letter printed and sent to the government offices of the whole province for reference, so as to encourage and spur them. This letter was later included in the book The Imperial Statecraft Compendium, and was recited by the world.

When Leshan Gong was in Hengshan, he often went to the prison to treat the prisoners without charge. When his son became rich and illustrious, Leshan Gong was already over eighty, and yet he still often went to the prison to visit the sick and treat them without charge. The county magistrate, seeing that he was old, sent someone to decline on his behalf; he replied: “Saving people is my most joyful thing.”

When Leshan Gong was eighty-four, his son Xiantao resigned his office and returned home because his stepmother had died, and because his father was far advanced in age, he decided never to take office again. Late one night, when snow was falling thick and fast, the family of a sick person knocked at the door, seeking a physician to go out to a consultation. Xiantao rose and opened the door, and said to the messenger: “My father is old, and in the dead of night it is inconvenient to disturb him; could you come again tomorrow morning?” Unexpectedly, at this moment Leshan Gong had already heard the voice and, putting on a coat, had risen from bed. He called Xiantao into the inner room and said to him: “This is most likely an urgent case of childbirth — how can the treatment be delayed?” Then he put on his wooden clogs and went with the messenger to the consultation. The profound seriousness of this sentiment of giving up oneself to save others is truly admirable.

Therefore Heaven has eyes and sees the merest detail, and the retribution it gave to Leshan Gong was especially abundant. Accordingly, when Leshan Gong was ninety-three, his grandson Zhaokui took second place in the provincial examination of the renzi year of the Qianlong reign. He had seven great-grandsons: Gaomin and Tiemin were both Hanlin scholars and assumed the offices of chief examiner and education commissioner; Suimin and Yumin were both juren and served as county magistrates; Jingmin, after passing the bagong examination, was assigned to serve in the Grand Council; while Zhenmin served in the capital as an official, and Sanmin was selected as a filial-and-incorrupt upright man. The people of the time honoured them as the “Seven Masters of Hengshan.”

On the seventieth birthday of the great-great-great-grandmother, the Honourable Lady Kang, the famous scholar Ruan Wenda of the time presented a congratulatory couplet: “The southern peak gathers the blessing, the southern chant spreads the grace; at seventy the longevity is celebrated, and seven sons have all gained fame.” The wording of the couplet was apt and fitting — truly a beautiful tale among people!

My grandfather, Yifeng Gong, was the great-great-grandson of Leshan Gong. After passing the Hanlin examination in the guichou year of the Xianfeng reign, he successively served as magistrate of Shicheng and Xinhui in Guangdong Province, prefect of Gaozhou Prefecture, and was recommended for the post of intendant. And he held office with integrity, was wholehearted in the affairs of the people, and brought benefit to the localities. Toward the great cases of armed feuds that occurred at the time he dealt leniently, preserving many lives, and accumulated abundant virtue. The common people even established a living shrine to commemorate him, showing the degree of respect he enjoyed.

In private I have often contemplated the meaning of Mencius's saying, “The grace of a gentleman lasts five generations and then is cut off.” The sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons of Leshan Gong all for four generations passed examinations and held office; and at the fifth generation, Yifeng Gong too was still able to actively do good and accumulate virtue, and to carry forward the bequeathed virtue of the ancestors; and by the time of my father, the Grand Coordinator Gong, it was even more honoured and distinguished. I myself have the honour to be the seventh generation, and still receive the sheltering grace of Leshan Gong; so it may be said that Leshan Gong's abundant virtue, in blessing his descendants, has already surpassed the five generations of which Mencius spoke. In seeking out the cause, that Leshan Gong's medical skill was excellent and could save the lives of the sick was already not easy; and that with fine medical skill he could moreover make light of wealth and uphold righteousness, and sincerely save people, was the more difficult piled upon the difficult. Among the many famous physicians we have seen in various places, there are indeed many who, by practicing medicine, accumulated a great deal of wealth, even millions and hundreds of millions; but the number of those whose wealth has come down to the third generation is very small. And even if there is the occasional exception, it is inevitably a physician whose skill was exquisite and who moreover loved to do good and give. I truly wish I could meet several more such physicians who do good and save people appearing in the world — that would be the blessing of society! In recent times life has been harder, and the cost of medicine has been high; the poor and sick are mostly unable to afford treatment and medicine — this is precisely the best opportunity for the medical profession to arouse the heart to do good! Therefore I respectfully record here the old deeds of Leshan Gong in practicing medicine to save people, hoping to provide them to the virtuous of the medical profession as a reference for practicing medicine and saving people.

Now I would still like to add some analysis and supplementation. Leshan Gong's medical skill was excellent and he saved many people, yet when his shop was robbed he had to mortgage his house to repay the debt — from this one may know that his financial situation was indeed not good. When he was over eighty, and his son, a county magistrate, returned home, in the snowy dead of night he still wore wooden clogs and went out on foot to a consultation — from this we may know that Leshan Gong remained so poor in his old age! The Great Learning says: “The benevolent use wealth to build up their persons; the not-benevolent use their persons to build up wealth.” Physicians and medicine shops are occupations that build wealth, but if one treats the poor and sick without charge and gives them medicine, one will not grow rich. And yet although Leshan Gong could not grow rich, he was nevertheless able to build up his person, and won the unanimous esteem of society at the time — it may be said that his fame of virtue flourished in his own time and his name was handed down to posterity. Truly not easy! For five or six generations in succession his descendants passed the examinations and held office, and were noble and flourishing, precisely according to the saying “using wealth to build up one's person.”

And Leshan Gong and his son were both very poor. His grandson Zhaokui, that is, my great-great-grandfather, though he served as an instructor and managed the academy and had very many pupils, was nevertheless also very poor. Not only that — I once heard the elders say that when my great-grand-uncle was selected for the Hanlin, the good news, sent by swift post, reached the home from the capital, and my great-great-great-grandmother, the Honourable Lady Kang, was at the time holding her seventh son to her breast to nurse him; upon hearing the news she at once went in person into the kitchen to prepare a meal for the messenger — from this one may know the degree of the family's poverty!

My great-grandfather had served in the capital as an official, and after his death left no property whatsoever; therefore my grandfather, Yifeng Gong, was orphaned and poor from childhood, and when he studied in his mountain study he had to cook for himself. At forty-two he entered the Hanlin Academy. Afterwards he held the post of county magistrate in Guangdong Province for more than ten years; as an official he was incorrupt, self-possessed, and often donated from his income to promote all kinds of good works in the localities, for example: building infant asylums, inoculating against smallpox, repairing roads, building bridges, purchasing burial grounds, and interring exposed coffins. Therefore the savings he left behind after his death were not great, so in his early years my late father had to rely on the wages of his outside work to supply the household.
